paper_title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io

Introduction normals, and largely retain their editing abilities. Image generation models have become increasingly capable of producing realistic and coherent visual content [44, 102]. growing line of work argues that this capability reflects general visual understanding that can be utilized for perception tasks [35, 39, 40, 124]. Vision Banana [23] demonstrates that sufficiently capable image generator can be adapted into generalist visual perception model by rendering predictions as RGB images. It rivals domain specialists on segmentation and geometry while largely keeping the generators editing abilities. However, its base model, data and code are proprietary, so it is unclear which components account for these results. Does the paradigm transfer to publicly available image generators, and how do design choices not elaborated in the Vision Banana report affect the resulting model? We introduce Open Vision Banana (OVB) , fully reproducible recipe and set of models for generative visual perception. To derive this recipe, we systematically study the design choices that turn an image generator into perception model. As shown in Fig. 1, the analysis spans the type and composition of training data, target representations and prompt design, the choice of parameters to adapt, and inference-time readout (decoding generated RGB raw output to task specific final format). Our experiments show that these choices have large effects and can depend on one another. model may locate the right region yet score poorly because it paints the wrong color or breaks an output convention. In particular, low-level decisions such as the palette and prompt wording strongly affect accuracy. Supervision for one task can help or hurt others, and choices that help individually may no longer help when combined (Appendix E.2.4). Finally, we introduce legend ensembling, which segments an image under several randomly drawn color legends and fuses the passes by majority vote. Without retraining, it improves the zero-shot 9B model by up to 8.7 mIoU on Cityscapes and 15.0 mIoU on COCO-Object, with gains mostly from fixing colors bound to wrong classes. Open Vision Banana makes four main contributions: fully open recipe for adapting public image generators to four segmentation tasks, depth estimation, and surface normal estimation. The models are trained exclusively on public data, and we release the complete data pipeline, training code, and model checkpoints. Controlled experiments on performance-critical design choices, with an analysis of failure modes. Legend ensembling, training-free test-time scaling method for generator-based segmentation. Competitive open models that surpass Vision Banana on Cityscapes, come close to it on referring and reasoning segmentation, perform well on depth and surface2. Open Vision Banana Recipe OVB turns pretrained image generator into perception model without task-specific heads: given an input image and an instruction p, it generates an RGB image that deterministic, task-specific readout converts into prediction. 2.1. Base Generators We release fine-tuned FLUX.2-Klein models at 4B and 9B scale [44], open-weight generators that condition on an input image. All transformer parameters are trained, from the input and context embedders to the output layers. The VAE and text encoder stay frozen. 2.2. RGB Task Modeling Each task has deterministic encoder that renders an annotation as an RGB target and decoder that reads generated image back into prediction. Both use per-sample metadata such as the color legend, depth scaling and resizing. 2.2.1. Color Mapping for Segmentation Tasks Prompts specify colors as RGB triplets, hexadecimal codes (64 most-separated colors of 200-color palette, research question S2), or as one of 37 common color names. Black is reserved for background. Prompt templates and color notation vary across samples. Semantic segmentation. The prompt lists the requested classes with their colors. Colors are assigned at random for each sample, using the same procedure during training and inference. Given the classes present in an image, training examples request random subset in 70% of cases, all present classes in 15%, and subset augmented with absent negative classes in the remaining 15%  (Fig. 9)  . Negative classes teach the model not to hallucinate absent masks. The target paints each prompted class in its assigned color and leaves all other pixels black. At inference, each generated pixel is assigned to the nearest prompted color or to background. Instance segmentation. Each prompt names one category and lists 32 colors. We keep the 32 largest instances of the category, sort them by their leftmost pixel and paint the i-th instance in the i-th color (Appendix E.1.2). The fixed order makes training targets unique for each image and prompt. Evaluation matches predicted and ground-truth instances by overlap without penalizing alternative color assignments. The readout follows Vision Banana, adding color snapping, gap filling, and GrabCut refinement (Appendix B.2). Referring segmentation. Each prompt pairs the referring expression with color sampled independently from the named palette. The model renders the referred region in that color, which is converted to binary mask during readout. 2 2.2.2. Color Mapping for Geometry Tasks Depth. Following prior work [6, 38], depth is encoded as affine-invariant inverse depth: valid values are normalized per image to the RGB range and replicated across channels, so nearer points are brighter (figures use spectral colormap for readability). At inference, the prediction is mapped back to inverse depth and evaluated after per-image affine alignment. Surface normals. Normals are converted to common camera-space convention and each vector component is mapped linearly to one normalized RGB channel. At inference, the RGB prediction is mapped back to camera-space vectors and normalized to unit length. For both depth and surface-normal tasks, the prompts explicitly state the expected output representation. Further geometric encoding details are provided in Sec. B.1. 2.3. Public Data Mixture Vision Banana fine-tunes proprietary base model on proprietary vision data mixed with the base models original training data. We only use public datasets. We mix Perception data for the above tasks with replay data from public text-to-image, image-editing, and identity-reconstruction datasets. The resulting pools contain 2.1M training pairs for the zero-shot models and 3.8M for the non-zero-shot models (Appendix C.2). Appendix Tables 20 and 21 give the sampling weight for each task and the datasets and their shares within each task. 2.4. Training Because all targets are RGB images, we train with the base generators rectified-flow objective [55]. The only taskdependent element is the validity mask described below. We encode the target as zy, sample Gaussian noise ϵ and uniformly distributed interpolation coefficient (0, 1], and form zt = (1 t)zy + tϵ. Conditioned on the clean image and text prompt p, the transformer predicts ˆv = vθ(zt, t, p, x) with flow target ϵ zy. (1) LF = E(x,p,y),t,ϵ Geometry annotations contain undefined regions encoded by placeholder colors that model might learn to reproduce  (Fig. 13)  . Such regions account for about 8% of target pixels in the non-zero-shot pool and are therefore excluded from the loss using validity mask. Zero-shot models (2% invalid target regions) and non-geometry tasks use no mask and standard flow-matching. For masked training, the validity mask follows the image transforms and is area-resized 3 to the latent grid; positions with at least 50% valid coverage contribute to the loss. We use no erosion in the final models, exclude samples with no valid latent positions, and normalize each eligible sample by its valid area. The full-scale models are trained for 100K steps at global batch size of 192 on aspect-ratio buckets of about 5122 pixels (512512, 576448, 608416, and their transposes). We use AdamW [57] (weight decay 104), FSDP, and bf16 autocast with fp32 parameters, using constant learning rate after linear warmup: 5 106 (500 warmup steps) for 4B and 2106 (1,000 steps) for 9B. Each epoch draws 1M samples with replacement, split across tasks according to Appendix Table 20. Training thus spans about 19 epochs. Final models use weight-space averaging of few late transformer checkpoints (Appendix C.1). The nonzero-shot runs took about 73 on 16 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs (4B) and 79 on 32 (9B). 2.5. Evaluation Protocol and Data The evaluation protocol adopts standard metrics for each task and is specified in Appendix C.3. All models sample with 28 steps and guidance scale of 3.5. The datasets used for evaluation are listed in Appendix Table 21. 3. Evaluating Open Vision Banana Setup. We evaluate four OVB models, obtained by finetuning FLUX.2 Klein 4B and 9B under two data regimes. Following the dense-prediction literature [38, 40, 110, 128], zero-shot refers to datasets excluded from training, while the zerothe tasks themselves are seen during training: shot models are never trained on any evaluation benchmark. The non-zero-shot models additionally train on the training splits of some of the evaluation datasets (Appendix Table 21) and compute the geometry loss only on valid pixels (Sec. 2.4). Unless noted, segmentation uses the randomdraw protocol that re-samples classcolor assignments for every image. Legend ensembling and test-time scaling in brief. For semantic and instance segmentation, scores marked use legend ensembling (details in Sec. 3.4): passes with different color legends are fused by majority vote, and the mean single-pass score is given in parentheses. Analysis of Design Choices In this section, we analyze critical design choices during task definition, data acquisition, and model training to derive the final recipe for generative visual perception  (Fig. 1)  . Each analysis varies one factor and keeps other settings as described below. Training. The analyses use two reduced setups, one for segmentation and one for geometry. Each variant fine-tunes F2K9B Base with the full-scale 9B setup (Sec. 2.4) for 37.5K steps, at global batch size of 64 (segmentation) or 8 (geometry). segmentation run takes about 370 GPUhours on GH200 GPUs (23 on 16 GPUs), and geometry run about 80 GPU-hours on H200 GPUs (20 on 4 GPUs). Data. Training examples follow the segmentation and geometry mixtures in Appendix Table 20. Each epoch draws about 250K (segmentation) or 160K (geometry) samples, so the 2.4M and 300K samples seen during training amount to 9.6 and 1.9 epochs. Segmentation sampling is without replacement; geometry sampling follows source quotas and uses replacement when source is too small (Appendix C.2). Evaluation. Segmentation variants are evaluated on the segmentation benchmarks in Appendix Table 21. For the geometry ablations, we additionally report five evaluations of other tasks to check whether gain in depth or normals comes at the cost of the models other capabilities: Cityscapes mIoU (CS), COCO-Stuff mIoU (CO), RefCOCOg cIoU (RS), SA-Co/Gold-14K cgF1 (IS), and the ImgEdit UGE score (IE). Cityscapes and RefCOCOg use the full validation splits, and COCO-Stuff and SA-Co/Gold use fixed subsets (C.4). Appendix C.3 gives the full evaluation protocol. 4.1. Task Definition We first study how to express the tasks as RGB images. Additional analysis can be found in Appendix E. 8 RQ-S1. Which classcolor mappings let the model generalize and follow the prompt? Setup. To test whether model memorizes fixed class color mapping (e.g., carblue) or learns to follow the colors given in the prompt, we vary the mapping at training and evaluation time, using the 19 Cityscapes classes shared by all datasets in this experiment. Fixed colors (#1) always lists all 19 classes with fixed colorclass correspondences, random colors (#2) lists all 19 classes with new colors for every sample, and random subset (#3) lists only random subset of present classes, leaving unlisted regions black  (Fig. 9)  . Random colors are drawn from the 100 most-separated colors of our palette with minimum pairwise color difference of = 25 (Euclidean distance in CIELAB, CIE76), relaxed when too few colors satisfy it, or from the 37-color named palette when prompt uses color names (research question S2). Distance requirement is relaxed when fewer than required colors satisfy the filtering criteria. Each variant fine-tunes F2K9B Base for 6K steps at batch size 64 on 40K-sample pool of 25% semantic segmentation (BDD100K and ACDC), 25% identity reconstruction and 50% image editing. Analysis. As shown in Tab. 12, training with fixed colors performs well under the same evaluation protocol (53.9 mIoU), but collapses when the colors are varied at inference (7.1), indicating rigid memorization of the mapping. Training with random colors (#2) avoids this collapse and reaches 51.0 mIoU with unseen color assignments. In the set protocol, the prompt lists only subset of the classes and unrequested regions are not scored (Appendix C.3), so it tests whether the model follows the legend. Random subset performs best here (66.5 mIoU) but loses 15.0 mIoU under the random-draw (rd) protocol, where all Cityscapes classes are requested. Table 12 (S1). The recipe therefore combines random colors with mixture of subset, full-set and negativeclass prompts (adding absent classes). RQ-S2. What color palette best supports unambiguous color generation for semantic segmentation? Setup. We construct 200-color palette from Matplotlibs XKCD colors using farthest-point sampling in CIELAB space and order colors from most to least separated. We compare the full palette with its first 100, 64 and 32 colors and per-image variant that uses the most-separated colors, where is the number of classes present in the image, or the number of listed classes if the prompt adds absent ones. For each training and evaluation sample, colors are drawn from the corresponding palette and randomly assigned to the requested classes. Smaller palettes offer fewer colors but larger distances between them. Analysis. Restricting the palette to more widely separated colors generally improves segmentation over using all 200 colors, particularly on COCO-Stuff and COCO-Things. Shrinking the palette further does not always help: Top 32 improves Cityscapes but lowers both COCO benchmarks. How do image-generation and image-editing data affect geometry and retained capabilities? Setup. We vary the share of image-generation examples and, separately, editing and identity-reconstruction examples. Each share is set to zero, half its default, its default, or twice its default, with the remaining sampling probability redistributed across the other tasks. The defaults are 15% and 25%, respectively. All variants train for 50K steps. Analysis. No setting is best for all tasks, and trends are not monotonic (Tab. 14). Removing generation data gives the lowest normal error but worsens depth. Doubling it to 30% raises depth AbsRel from 0.061 to 0.063, slightly increases δ1 from 96.5% to 96.6%, and worsens both normal errors. Removing editing/identity data worsens both geometry tasks and sharply reduces editing retention. The variant without generation examples also gives the highest GenAIBench CLIPFlanT5 score in this sweep (0.8074 versus 0.7871 at the 15% default; Appendix Table 31(d)). Editing 9 Appendix E.3 studies low-rank adaptation of the 4B model as low-compute alternative: adapters of rank 64 128 match full fine-tuning on editing, depth and normals, but trail it by about 12 mIoU on semantic segmentation. Takeaway (A1). Updating more transformer parameters substantially improves segmentation and normal estimation. Depth accuracy is highest when only the embeddings remain frozen. 5. Related Work Pretrained image generators are increasingly used for visual perception, either by extracting their semantic and geometric features [108, 125] or by framing vision tasks directly as image prediction [4, 27, 95, 96]. Specialized models such as Marigold and Lotus further exploit generative priors for dense geometric prediction [32, 38], but do not aim at preserving the general-purpose generation abilities. More closely related are generalist models that unify generation and perception. DICEPTION [124], Jodi [109], OneDiffusion [46], and PixWizard [50] adapt diffusionbased generators to multiple vision tasks, while SenseNovaVision [31] and MODUS [113] build on unified multimodal architectures. Vision Banana [23] demonstrates strong multi-task perception through instruction-tuning proprietary image generator while retaining its generative capabilities. Other studies find that frozen generators can already solve some perception tasks out-of-the-box [54, 111]. OVB differs from these works in that every component is public and in its controlled analysis of critical design choices. An extended discussion is provided in Appendix A. 6. Conclusion Open Vision Banana is fully open recipe for turning pretrained image generators into unified segmentation and geometry models while largely preserving their editing abilities. Controlled experiments favor randomized, wellseparated color palettes, relative inverse depth, full transformer adaptation, and highlight trade-off between perception accuracy and retained generation quality. The resulting models are competitive across tasks, improve further with training-free legend ensembling, and yield stronger frozen features for object discovery and correspondence. Their main limitation is the weaker perception of open base models relative to proprietary generators such as Nano Banana Pro. sections.content: A. Extended Related Work Generative image models as visual priors. Image generators have evolved from text-to-image synthesis systems into flexible image-to-image engines through latent diffusion, transformer-based diffusion backbones, instruction tuning, and controllable conditioning [8, 71, 77, 104, 123]. This has motivated growing line of work that reuses generative priors to solve perception tasks instead of training separate discriminative models. Early diffusion-perception methods such as VPD [125], ODISE [108], and TADP [42] showed that pretrained diffusion features and denoising pipelines contain spatially aligned semantic and geometric information useful for segmentation, depth, and dense prediction. These methods typically train perception heads on the extracted features or modify the architecture, so the prediction is not produced by the generator itself. Vision tasks as image generation. second line of work frames vision tasks directly as image generation. Early methods show that masks, depth maps, and other perception outputs can be represented as RGB images [24, 27, 96, 98]. More recent contributions exploit strong visual priors acquired by generative foundation models during large-scale pretraining for dense prediction, mostly depth and surface normals [22, 28, 32, 33, 38, 39, 94, 106, 112]. Several concurrent works study segmentation-specific uses of generative models [1, 40, 92, 117]. These models usually address one or few tasks and do not try to preserve or evaluate general image generation. Unified generation and understanding. The idea of unifying heterogeneous vision tasks through shared imagespace prediction interface predates the recent wave of generative foundation models. Early works such as Visual Prompting via Image Inpainting [4] and Painter [95] formulated diverse computer-vision tasks as image prediction. More recently, this idea has been revisited in the context of pretrained generative models that unify generation and understanding. DICEPTION [124] is one of the closest open baselines, using color-encoded perception targets in diffusion model. Vision Banana [23] demonstrates that instruction-tuning Nano Banana Pro on vision-task data can turn generator into strong generalist perception model without sacrificing its original generation abilities. Generally, unified multimodal systems differ mainly in the generative backbone they adapt. Jodi [109], OneDiffusion [46], PixWizard [50], and UniPercept [126] build on diffusionor flow-based image generators and model perception outputs as images, labels, or task-specific visual representations. SenseNova-Vision [31] and MODUS [113] instead adapt BAGEL-style [16] unified multimodal decoders, combining autoregressive text generation with shared flow-matching visual generation pathway for producing dense RGB outputs through VAE latents. Relatedly, RINO [111] and other recent works [18, 54] show that off-the-shelf image generation or editing models already possess substantial denseprediction capabilities without perception-specific adaptation or retraining, though they typically underperform tuned approaches and rely on adjusted evaluation protocols to become competitive. C.2. Training data Table 21 lists the full-scale training pool and the evaluation datasets, and Table 20 gives the per-task sampling weights of the full-scale (OVB) and ablation mixtures. Full-scale training data. The zero-shot OVB models use the non-underlined sources in Table 21, excluding targetbenchmark training splits and evaluation images. The five geometry sources (Synscapes, Replica, Matterport3D, Hypersim and Taskonomy) cover rendered street scenes and synthetic, reconstructed and scanned interiors. We convert all sources to the conventions of Sec. B.1. Non-zero-shot models also use the underlined sources and their training splits, which grows the pool from 2.1M to 3.8M training pairs. For VKITTI2, training uses non-clone renderings of the five scenes used for normal evaluation. Training and test images therefore show the same scenes under different rendering conditions. For geometry sources added to the non-zero-shot pool, we identify contiguous border rows and columns with at least half their pixels invalid. We crop these from the image, target and mask, unless the crop would remove more than 20 25% at any edge or retain less than 60% of the image area. After this step, we discard examples with more than 25% invalid area. Remaining invalid regions inside the image are excluded from the loss by the validity mask. The non-zero-shot Replica pool contains 3,341 upright views rendered with mesh vertex colors; the zero-shot models use the earlier pool. For the added ScanNet source, we fit local planes to depth to obtain normals and orient them toward the camera. Released manifests record source versions, counts, image IDs and crop coordinates. Ablation training data. The ablations draw from smaller subsets of the zero-shot pool and follow the same exclusions. Segmentation ablations use no geometry data. They use the non-underlined 2D sources but leave out Hypersim (semantic and instance segmentation) as well as RailSem19 and Trans10K-v2 (semantic segmentation). Referring segmentation uses 150K samples from Visual Genome (without COCO images) and Mapillary Vistas. Geometry ablations restrict the 2D tasks to ACDC, BDD100K, ADE20K, and PASCAL VOC for semantic segmentation and to ADE20K, Mapillary Vistas, and PASCAL VOC for instance segmentation. The depth and normal weights are each split equally among the five nonunderlined geometry sources. The depthand normalprompt variants of the prompt study assign the full 30% geometry share to single geometry task. Editing replay uses the first 50K valid Pico-Banana pairs after shuffling, identity replay uses 10K of their source images as both input and target, and text-to-image replay uses 500K PD12M examples. All three selections use seed 42. Each geometry-ablation epoch draws 160K examples across all tasks according to the task weights. C.3. Evaluation details and metrics Our evaluation protocol follows Vision Banana [23] where applicable and extends it to broader benchmark suite. The exact datasets used for evaluation are listed in Table 21. Generation. We compare each final model with its base generator using matched inference and judging settings, with 28 steps and guidance 3.5. GenAI-Bench [47] uses VQAScore with the CLIPFlanT5 [XXL] judge, for the final models and the geometry ablations alike (IG-C, Table 31); ImgEdit-Bench [114] uses ImgEdit-Judge. Both results are averaged over three generation seeds. Editing uses fixed assignment to 16 logical shards because the noise generator advances between examples within each shard. Semantic segmentation. Mean intersection-over-union (mIoU), computed as the arithmetic mean of the per-class IoUs is used for evaluation. We consider three evaluation protocols. Fixed uses the complete dataset taxonomy with its canonical classcolor mapping. Random-draw (rd) retains the complete taxonomy but samples new classcolor mapping for each image, thereby measuring generalization across colors. Set requests random subset of the classes present in each image and assigns them random colors. Its size is drawn uniformly between 1 and one fewer than the number of present classes, or is 1 if only one class is present. Only the requested classes are scored and pixels of other classes are ignored, so this protocol measures how accurately the model paints the requested classes, without penalizing painting in unrequested regions. Unless otherwise stated, we use random-draw evaluation throughout the paper. Referring segmentation. Following LISA [45], we report cumulative IoU (cIoU), the summed foreground intersection divided by the summed foreground union over all queries, and gIoU, the mean per-query foreground IoU. cIoU weights queries by their union area, whereas gIoU gives every query equal weight. Instance segmentation. We use the official SA-Co/Gold evaluator of SAM 3, as Vision Banana does. It retains only queries that are instance-exhaustive in all three oracle annotations. Each decoded instance (Sec. B.2) is exported as binary COCO RLE mask with confidence 1.0, so the evaluators 0.5 score threshold discards nothing. Queries that the VLM presence gate judges absent receive no prediction, Vision Banana filters queries the same way with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite. For each query, we score the same predictions against all three annotations and keep the result with the highest local F1, averaged over the IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05. An empty prediction for an empty target counts as perfect. Evaluation uses all groundtruth instances, without the training cap of 32. Positive micro-F1 (pmF1) measures instance matching and mask localization on positive queries. Image-level Matthews correlation coefficient (IL-MCC) measures category-presence accuracy. Within each subset, cgF1 = pmF1 IL-MCC, so hallucinated predictions on negative queries are penalized. We average each metric over the seven subsets, so mean cgF1 need not equal mean pmF1 times mean ILMCC. Geometry. Table 22 lists the final evaluation splits.
